• Other names: Needle leaf Ludwigia, Narrow-leaf Ludwigia
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Optimal GH: soft to moderately hard water
  • Substrate: nutrient-rich
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth form: stem
  • Growth rate: slow to moderate (submersed), moderate (emersed)
  • Placement: midground and background
  • Size: up to 50 cm without trimming
  • CO2: needed
  • Propagation: cut off the top shoots
  • Colour: green to reddish

• Supplements: needs CO2 for robust growth.
  • Growth: CO2 and liquid fertilizers help it grow fuller and bushier.
  • Pruning: trim overgrown stems to keep it compact. Snip the tops a few inches off and discard; this encourages side shoots.
  • Water changes: avoid drastic changes; make them gradually and regularly, which also limits nitrates.

Planting: separate the stems gently and plant groups of two or three stems in a nutrient-rich substrate under bright light. It can grow aerial roots; cut above the node and stick it in the substrate.

Propagation: take sizeable cuttings from the stems and place them in the substrate. Remove the leaves from the last node at the lower end to encourage rooting.

Alternative: the Dry Start Method (DSM) boosts the development of slow-growing plants, cycles the substrate and removes algae problems. The plant also suits paludariums. The transition from emersed to submerged form generally takes a couple of weeks to a month.

Temperature: 20 – 28 °C. The plant dislikes cold water and melts easily; very warm water makes leaves smaller. Submerged leaves formed at 23 °C were clearly narrower than those formed at 31 °C; light intensity and pH did not affect leaf shape in the same experiments.

Hardness: grows in both hard and soft water, but soft to moderately hard is best.

pH: 5.5 – 7.5; it prefers slightly acidic water.

Fertilization: colour deepens with low nitrates (less than 20 ppm). It does not need high iron to turn red.

If you keep shrimp with it, note that high CO2 and copper (found in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Tank size: a 40 L tank is adequate for a few clumps. Despite its height, its slow growth makes it suitable even for small tanks.

Lighting: medium to high light with higher PAR, for at least 10 hours daily, brings out intense red colour and bushy growth. Leaves turn redder in high light and stay green in dim light. It is not suited to low-tech tanks.

Substrate: nutrient-rich substrates (such as ADA Amazonia) are best, as they help preserve the colour of the stem, underleaf and leaf tips.

CO2: supplementation is highly recommended; it is very difficult to grow without CO2. High-light plants must be balanced in CO2 and nutrients, otherwise algae will appear.

Ludwigia arcuata is a species of aquatic stem plant in the family Onagraceae and genus Ludwigia, a genus of about 82 species native to Central, North and South America. It grows in marshes, ponds and ditches in the southeastern United States, mainly South Carolina, Florida and Georgia, both on land (emersed) and underwater (submerged).

The shoots are green to reddish with narrow, pointed, needle-like leaves that range from green to orange to red. It can reach 50 cm. The emersed form is branching, can lie flat, has green round leaves and small bright yellow flowers, and is sturdy. The submerged form grows upwards, with leaves 2.5 – 4 cm long and 4 mm wide, green to reddish-orange or reddish-brown, arranged in opposite pairs. It is less hardy than the emersed form.

It is difficult to turn red and is sensitive to parameter swings, so it is not recommended for beginners, unless kept emersed in a paludarium. Benefits: suits Dutch-style aquascapes, does not overshadow other plants, gives cover for fish, fry and shrimp, provides biofilm for fry and shrimplets, and oxygenates the water.

Problems

  • Melting: after transfer from emersed to submerged growth the plant sheds leaves; wait and it will regrow.
  • Not red: the best recommendation is soft water, nutrient-rich substrate, strong light, CO2 and low nitrates. Excess iron will not make it red.
  • Very slow growth: caused by inadequate nutrients or light.
  • Discoloration: may be caused by iron or other nutrient deficiency; dose liquid fertilizer regularly.
  • Pests: emersed plants may carry pond snails, slugs and filamentous algae; disinfect or quarantine first.
  • Deformity: lower stems and leaves may shrivel, often due to unstable or insufficient CO2 and inadequate nutrients.
